source_caption:
To finally secure the green light for his deeply controversial, fiercely personal passion project, director Martin Scorsese had to strike a massive, career-altering bargain with Universal Pictures. The studio only agreed to finance the heavily protested film on a severely restricted budget of just $7 million, forcing Scorsese to shoot the sprawling epic in a frantic 58 days in Morocco. In exchange for this financial risk, Scorsese had to legally promise the studio that his very next project would be a highly commercial, guaranteed mainstream hit—a promise he ultimately kept by directing the wildly successful 1991 thriller Cape Fear. By treating the old Hollywood adage of “one for them, one for me” as a literal contract, Scorsese masterfully proves that making a fiercely uncompromising artistic masterpiece sometimes requires a shrewd, deeply pragmatic business deal.
⠀
The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), directed by Martin Scorsese, starring Willem Dafoe, Harvey Keitel, Barbara Hershey. A deeply conflicted, fiercely human Jesus of Nazareth struggles with overwhelming self-doubt, profound fear, and the agonizing weight of his divine destiny, culminating in a profoundly controversial vision of a normal, earthly life completely free of crucifixion.

source_details.title: The Last Temptation of Christ
source_details.synopsis: The Last Temptation of Christ is a 1988 epic religious drama film directed by Martin Scorsese. Written by Paul Schrader, with uncredited rewrites from Scorsese and Jay Cocks, it is an adaptation of Nikos Kazantzakis' controversial 1955 novel of the same name. The film, starring Willem Dafoe, Harvey Keitel, Barbara Hershey, Andre Gregory, Harry Dean Stanton and David Bowie, was shot entirely in Morocco. The film depicts the life of Jesus Christ and his struggle with various forms of temptation including fear, doubt, depression, reluctance and lust.
